blocks.html: Sometime in June, I came across Aaed Musa's YouTube channel. He made a video a couple months back showcasing his design of a 3-D printed planetary gearbox. What blew my mind was that it was all 3-D printed. I loved the flexibility of being able to design and make all the parts in-house (literally), and I thought creating a 3-D printed actuator would make for a worthwhile endeavor. Initially, I did not have a clear goal of the actuator, other than that it would hopefully lead into a robot leg of sorts.
My first real design inspiration came from MIT's mini cheetah paper. This design chose to house the ring gear inside of the stator, which allows for an extremely compact design.
After some initial inspiration, I set out and found an electric motor similar to the specs given by the MIT paper. The specs are as follows:

The initial idea was to disassemble the stator wiring completely from the motor. In doing so, I can design a planetary gearbox that goes inside the inner diameter of the stator. However, after hours of trying to remove the stator, the stator wouldn't budge at all. So I ended up settling on placing the ring gear right above the stator. In doing so, the rotor would have to be redesigned. This was a bad design choice looking back. The rotor is wayyy too long to provide reliable operation given the airgap between the rotor and stator was only a couple mm.

As for my gear ratio, I decided to mimic MIT's gear ratio of 6:1. To calculate the number of teeth, I just had to apply a couple of equations. The first being: S/(S+R) where S = number of teeth on sun gear and R = number of teeth on ring gear, S = number of teeth on sun gear. To calculate the number of teeth on planets required this equation: R = 2 * P + S, where R and S are the same as above and P = number of teeth on planet gear. Also, one last equation is important if you want your planet gears to be evenly spaced around the sun: (R+S) / N where R and S are the same and N = the number of planets (3 in my case). I chose a gear module of 1 (which means that the diameter of my gears is equal to the teeth on the gears). My final design numbers were R = 80, P = 32, and S = 16. Notice that the inner diameter of the ring gear was almost the same size as the outer diameter of the electric motor. I convinced myself that the sun gear should have at least 10+ teeth for good measure, and that the ring gear was going on top of the stator anyways. Another bad design choice I made was I used double herringbone gears for my gearbox. In theory, they are the best gears to use, but they are a PAIN to assemble in practice.
